A wave repeats itself in **two independent ways**, and that is what "doubly periodic" means.

**Periodic in time.** Fix attention on one particle of the medium. It oscillates about its rest position, and after every interval equal to the period \(T\) it returns to exactly the same state of oscillation — the same displacement moving in the same direction. So at any one location the wave motion repeats itself at equal intervals of time.

**Periodic in space.** Now freeze the wave at one instant and look along it. The form of the wave repeats at equal distances: particles separated by one wavelength \(\lambda\) are in the same state of vibration, differing in phase by \(2\pi^{c}\). So at any given instant the wave is periodic in space.

The two periodicities are displayed by the two graphs of Fig. 8.1: displacement plotted against distance along the wave (period \(\lambda\)) and displacement plotted against time for one particle (period \(T\)). Because the motion repeats both in time and in space, wave motion is called a doubly periodic phenomenon.

**Doppler effect is the apparent change in the frequency of sound caused by relative motion between the source of sound and the listener.**

When a source and a listener are in motion relative to each other, the frequency of sound heard by the listener is not the same as the frequency actually emitted by the source. If the two approach each other the recorded frequency is higher than the emitted one; if they recede from each other it is lower. The effect appears whenever there is relative motion — whether the source moves, the listener moves, or both move.

The familiar example is an approaching train: the pitch of its whistle is noticeably higher as it comes towards you and drops as it passes and moves away, although the whistle itself is sounding one steady note throughout.

The effect was first identified in 1842 by the Austrian physicist Christian Doppler (1803-1853), after whom it is named. It is a wave phenomenon and so holds for electromagnetic waves as well as for sound.

**A transverse wave is a wave in which the particles of the medium vibrate in a direction perpendicular to the direction of propagation of the wave.**

Water waves are transverse: the water molecules vibrate perpendicular to the water surface while the wave itself travels along the surface.

Its main characteristics are:

1. All particles of the medium in the path of the wave vibrate perpendicular to the direction of propagation, with the same period and the same amplitude.
2. As the wave passes, the medium is divided into alternate **crests** (regions of positive displacement) and **troughs** (regions of negative displacement).
3. A crest and an adjacent trough together form one cycle of the wave; the distance between any two consecutive points in the same phase (crest to crest, or trough to trough) is the wavelength.
4. Crests and troughs advance through the medium and are responsible for the transfer of energy.
5. Transverse waves travel through solids and on the surfaces of liquids only — they cannot travel through the body of liquids or through gases, because the medium must possess **elasticity of shape**. (Electromagnetic waves are transverse but need no material medium.)
6. There is no change in pressure or density at any point of the medium as the wave passes; only its shape changes periodically.
7. If the vibrations of all the particles are confined to a single plane the wave is said to be **polarised** — transverse waves can be polarised.

**A wave in which the particles of the medium vibrate in a direction parallel to the direction of propagation of the wave is called a longitudinal wave.**

Sound waves are longitudinal waves.

Because the vibration is along the line of travel, the medium is divided into alternate **compressions** — regions where the particles are crowded together, so the pressure and density are high — and **rarefactions**, regions where the particles are more widely separated, so the pressure and density are low. A compression and the adjacent rarefaction together make one cycle of the wave, and the distance between any two consecutive points in the same phase is its wavelength.

For a longitudinal wave the medium needs only **elasticity of volume**, which solids, liquids and gases all possess, so longitudinal waves travel through all three; they cannot travel through vacuum or free space. Since the direction of vibration and the direction of propagation are the same, a longitudinal wave **cannot be polarised**.

Newton reasoned that since sound travels through a medium as a succession of compressions and rarefactions — the density being greater at a compression and smaller at a rarefaction — its speed must be governed by the **elasticity** and the **density** of the medium. He therefore wrote

\[\mathrm{v} = \sqrt{\dfrac{E}{\rho}}\]

where \(E\) is the appropriate modulus of elasticity of the medium and \(\rho\) is its density.

Newton further assumed that the temperature of the medium does not change during the passage of sound, i.e. that the propagation is an **isothermal** process. The volume elasticity of a gas under an isothermal change (the isothermal bulk modulus) is equal to the pressure \(P\) of the gas, so for air his formula becomes

\[\mathrm{v} = \sqrt{\dfrac{P}{\rho}}\]

This is Newton's formula for the velocity of sound in air.

**At constant temperature a change in pressure has no effect on the velocity of sound in air.**

By Laplace's formula the speed in air is \(\mathrm{v} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma P}{\rho}}\). Writing the density as \(\rho = \dfrac{M}{V}\), where \(M\) is the mass and \(V\) the volume of the air considered,

\[\mathrm{v} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma P V}{M}}\]

At constant temperature Boyle's law makes the product \(PV\) a constant; \(M\) and \(\gamma\) are constants too. Hence the whole expression under the root is constant and \(\mathrm{v}\) does not change, however the pressure is varied. Physically, raising the pressure of a gas at fixed temperature raises its density in exactly the same proportion, and the two effects cancel in the ratio \(P/\rho\).

The same conclusion follows from the ideal gas equation \(PV = nRT\), which turns the formula into

\[\mathrm{v} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma n R T}{M}}\]

Here the pressure has disappeared altogether and only the temperature is left. So for a gaseous medium obeying the ideal gas equation, a change in pressure alters the velocity of sound **only if it is accompanied by a change in temperature**.

**The speed of sound in air increases as the air becomes more moist (more humid).**

Humidity is the water vapour present in air. Let \(\rho_m\) and \(\rho_d\) be the densities of moist and dry air, and \(\mathrm{v}_m\) and \(\mathrm{v}_d\) the corresponding speeds of sound. Using Laplace's formula at the same pressure,

\[\mathrm{v}_m = \sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma P}{\rho_m}} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \mathrm{v}_d = \sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma P}{\rho_d}}\]

\[\therefore \dfrac{\mathrm{v}_m}{\mathrm{v}_d} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\rho_d}{\rho_m}}\]

Water vapour is lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen it displaces, so **moist air is always less dense than dry air**: at \(0\,^\circ\)C, \(\rho_m = 0.81\) kg/m\(^3\) against \(\rho_d = 1.29\) kg/m\(^3\). Hence \(\rho_m < \rho_d\), the ratio under the root exceeds 1, and

\[\mathrm{v}_m > \mathrm{v}_d\]

That is, sound travels faster in moist air than in dry air, and its speed increases with increasing moistness of the air.

**An echo is the repetition of the original sound caused by its reflection from some rigid surface lying at a distance from the source of sound.** Shouting in a hilly region and hearing the shout returned is the everyday example.

An echo is not heard everywhere, because the ear must be able to separate the reflected sound from the original. Our brain retains a sound for about **0.1 second**, so the reflected sound has to arrive more than 0.1 s after the original was produced if it is to be heard as a distinct repetition rather than merging with it.

Taking the speed of sound in air at \(22\,^\circ\)C as 344 m/s, the distance covered in that time is

\[\text{distance} = \text{speed} \times \text{time} = 344 \times 0.1 = 34.4\,\mathrm{m}\]

This is the **round trip**, so the reflecting surface must be at least half of it — about **17.2 m** — away from the source. Since the speed of sound depends on temperature, this minimum distance changes slightly with temperature.

If the reflecting surface is nearer than about 15 m the reflected sound joins on to the original instead of repeating it, and the result is reverberation rather than an echo.

Acoustics — the branch of physics dealing with the production, transmission and reception of sound — has applications well beyond human hearing. Any two of the following:

1. **SONAR** (SOund Navigational Ranging): a pulse of ultrasonic sound is transmitted into water and the reflected pulse detected. The time delay between transmission and reception gives the depth or distance of the object, which makes it useful for measuring the motion and position of submerged objects such as submarines.

2. **Ultrasonic medical imaging**: ultrasonic waves reflected from regions inside the body are used for prenatal examination, for detecting anomalous conditions such as tumours, and for studying the action of heart valves.

3. **Treatment of kidney stones**: high pressure, high amplitude shock waves produced outside the body are focused by a reflector or acoustic lens onto the stone; when the resulting stress exceeds the stone's tensile strength it breaks into small pieces that can be passed easily, without invasive surgery.

4. **Design of auditoria and concert halls**, where absorption and reflection are controlled so that sound is heard loudly and clearly at every seat, free of echo and reverberation.

5. **Noise control** in the design of quiet mass transit vehicles, which requires study of the generation and propagation of sound in the wheels and supporting structures.

6. **Geological survey**: reflected and refracted elastic waves passing through the Earth's interior reveal its properties and local anomalies such as oil deposits.

**Amplitude (\(A\))**: the amplitude of a wave motion is the largest displacement of a particle of the medium through which the wave is propagating, measured from its rest (equilibrium) position. Its SI unit is the **metre**.

**Wavelength (\(\lambda\))**: the wavelength is the distance between two successive particles of the medium which are in the same state of vibration — that is, particles having the same displacement and the same direction of velocity, whose phases therefore differ by \(2\pi^{c}\). Equivalently it is the distance between two consecutive crests or two consecutive troughs of a transverse wave, or between two consecutive compressions or rarefactions of a longitudinal wave. It too is measured in **metre**.

[Textbook note: the honest answer to this question is a DRAWING — it asks the reader to draw a wave and mark points in phase, out of phase, and a quarter-cycle apart. The answer above describes the construction and gives the phase-difference rule \(\Delta\phi = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x\) so the row stands alone, but it is a candidate for an authored solution diagram.]

Draw one full sinusoidal wave (two complete cycles are easier to label), plotting the displacement of the particles of the medium against distance along the wave, and mark the following on it.

**Points in phase.** Two particles are in phase when they have the **same displacement and the same direction of velocity** at that instant — they are then in identical states of oscillation. Successive particles satisfying this are separated by one wavelength \(\lambda\), and their phases differ by \(2\pi^{c}\). So mark **two successive crests** (or two successive troughs, or two consecutive points where the curve crosses the axis rising): they are one wavelength apart and are in phase. In Fig. 8.1 (a) of the chapter, particles \(B\) and \(F\) are such a pair.

**Points out of phase.** Mark a **crest and the trough next to it**. They are separated by \(\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\), so their phase difference is

\[\Delta\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \times \dfrac{\lambda}{2} = \pi^{c} = 180^\circ\]

One is at its maximum positive displacement while the other is at its maximum negative displacement — they are in exactly opposite states.

**Points with a phase difference of \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).** A phase difference of \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) corresponds to a path difference of

\[\Delta x = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi} \times \dfrac{\pi}{2} = \dfrac{\lambda}{4}\]

so mark a **crest and the neighbouring point where the curve crosses the axis** — a quarter of a wavelength apart. One is at maximum displacement with zero velocity, the other at zero displacement moving with maximum speed.

The general rule used throughout is that a path difference \(\Delta x\) corresponds to a phase difference \(\Delta\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\,\Delta x\).

The velocity of a wave is the distance it covers per unit time. During one period \(T\) the wave advances through exactly one wavelength \(\lambda\), so

\[\text{magnitude of velocity} = \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{time}} = \dfrac{\text{wavelength}}{\text{period}}\]

\[\mathrm{v} = \dfrac{\lambda}{T}\]

But the frequency is the reciprocal of the period, \(n = \dfrac{1}{T}\), and therefore

\[\boxed{\mathrm{v} = n\lambda}\]

**The velocity of a wave equals the product of its frequency and its wavelength.**

Two consequences follow. In a given medium the magnitude of the velocity is constant, so an increase in the frequency of a wave causes a proportionate decrease in its wavelength. And when a wave passes from one medium into another its frequency — fixed by the source — does not change, so the speed and the wavelength change together, in the same ratio.

**Statement.** When two or more waves travelling through a medium arrive at a point of the medium simultaneously, each wave produces its own displacement at that point independently of the others, and the resultant displacement at that point is equal to the **vector sum** of the displacements due to all the individual waves.

**Explanation.** Waves do not display any repulsion towards one another, so two wave patterns can overlap in the same region of space without affecting each other. Each wave carries on as though the other were not there; what is added is only their effect at each point. If \(\vec{y}_1\) and \(\vec{y}_2\) are the displacements that the two waves would separately produce at a point at a given instant, the resultant displacement there is

\[\vec{y} = \vec{y}_1 + \vec{y}_2\]

and for several waves \(\vec{y} = \vec{y}_1 + \vec{y}_2 + \vec{y}_3 + \cdots\)

Because the addition is **vector** addition, the two displacements reinforce each other where they are in the same direction and cancel wholly or partly where they are in opposite directions. This additive rule is what is meant by the principle of superposition of waves, and it is the basis of the phenomena of interference, beats and stationary waves. After the waves have crossed, each emerges unchanged in shape, frequency and amplitude.

Let \(n_0\) be the frequency emitted by the source, \(n\) the apparent (recorded) frequency, \(\mathrm{v}\) the speed of sound in the medium, \(\mathrm{v}_s\) the speed of the source and \(\mathrm{v}_L\) the speed of the listener. The general expression when both are in motion is

\[n = n_0\left[\dfrac{\mathrm{v} \pm \mathrm{v}_L}{\mathrm{v} \mp \mathrm{v}_s}\right]\]

where the **upper** signs (in both numerator and denominator) are used during relative approach and the **lower** signs during relative recede.

**i) Source and listener moving towards each other** — this is relative approach, so the upper signs apply:

\[n = n_0\left[\dfrac{\mathrm{v} + \mathrm{v}_L}{\mathrm{v} - \mathrm{v}_s}\right]\]

The numerator is increased and the denominator decreased, so \(n > n_0\) — the recorded frequency is higher than the emitted one.

**ii) Source and listener moving away from each other** — this is relative recede, so the lower signs apply:

\[n = n_0\left[\dfrac{\mathrm{v} - \mathrm{v}_L}{\mathrm{v} + \mathrm{v}_s}\right]\]

Now the numerator is decreased and the denominator increased, so \(n < n_0\) — the recorded frequency is lower than the emitted one.

Here the source is at rest, so \(\mathrm{v}_s = 0\), and only the listener moves with speed \(\mathrm{v}_L\). Putting \(\mathrm{v}_s = 0\) in the general expression \(n = n_0\left[\dfrac{\mathrm{v} \pm \mathrm{v}_L}{\mathrm{v} \mp \mathrm{v}_s}\right]\):

**1) Listener moving towards the source** (relative approach, upper sign):

\[n = n_0\left[\dfrac{\mathrm{v} + \mathrm{v}_L}{\mathrm{v}}\right]\]

Since the numerator exceeds \(\mathrm{v}\), the apparent frequency \(n\) is **greater** than the emitted frequency \(n_0\). Physically, the listener runs into the oncoming wavefronts and so meets more of them per second than a stationary listener would.

**2) Listener moving away from the source** (relative recede, lower sign):

\[n = n_0\left[\dfrac{\mathrm{v} - \mathrm{v}_L}{\mathrm{v}}\right]\]

Now the numerator is less than \(\mathrm{v}\), so the apparent frequency \(n\) is **less** than \(n_0\): the listener is running away from the wavefronts and fewer of them overtake per second.

Here the listener is at rest, so \(\mathrm{v}_L = 0\), and only the source moves with speed \(\mathrm{v}_s\). Putting \(\mathrm{v}_L = 0\) in the general expression \(n = n_0\left[\dfrac{\mathrm{v} \pm \mathrm{v}_L}{\mathrm{v} \mp \mathrm{v}_s}\right]\):

**i) Source moving towards the listener** (relative approach, so the denominator takes the minus sign):

\[n = n_0\left[\dfrac{\mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{v} - \mathrm{v}_s}\right]\]

The denominator is smaller than \(\mathrm{v}\), so \(n > n_0\) — the apparent frequency is higher. Physically, the source chases its own waves, so successive crests are emitted from points closer together and the wavelength reaching the listener is shortened.

**ii) Source moving away from the listener** (relative recede, so the denominator takes the plus sign):

\[n = n_0\left[\dfrac{\mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{v} + \mathrm{v}_s}\right]\]

Now the denominator exceeds \(\mathrm{v}\), so \(n < n_0\) — the apparent frequency is lower, the successive crests being emitted from points further apart.

**The state of oscillation of a particle of the medium is called its phase.**

To describe the phase of a particle at a place completely, three things must be known:

1. its **displacement** from the equilibrium position,
2. the **direction of its velocity**, and
3. the **oscillation number**, i.e. which oscillation the particle is currently performing.

The first two are needed because two particles may share the same displacement and still be in different states: in Fig. 8.1 (a) the particles \(P\) and \(Q\) have the same displacement but their velocities are oppositely directed, so they are not in the same phase. The third is needed because two particles may agree in both displacement and velocity direction and yet be one or more complete oscillations apart — particles \(B\) and \(F\), which are in phase, differ by 1 in their oscillation number.

The most convenient way to express phase is as an **angle**. For a sinusoidal wave the displacement varies as a sine function of distance and of time, so an angle can be assigned to each state of oscillation. Taking the phase angle of the particle the disturbance has just reached as \(0^\circ\), a particle that has completed a quarter of an oscillation and reached its positive maximum has phase \(\dfrac{\pi^{c}}{2} = 90^\circ\), one that has completed half an oscillation has phase \(\pi^{c}\,(180^\circ)\), and one that has completed a full oscillation has phase \(2\pi^{c}\,(360^\circ)\).

Two particles separated by one wavelength differ in phase by \(2\pi^{c}\); in general a path difference \(\Delta x\) corresponds to a phase difference \(\Delta\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\,\Delta x\). In the wave equation \(y(x,t) = a\sin(kx - \omega t + \phi)\) the whole argument \((kx - \omega t + \phi)\) is the phase of the particle at \(x\) at time \(t\).

[Textbook note: the question asks for FOUR properties of a progressive wave, and the chapter's own "Characteristics of progressive wave" list prints only TWO. The remaining two in the answer above are drawn from Secs. 8.1 and 8.2 — still this chapter's own text, but the section the question points at is thinner than the question assumes.]

**Definition.** A progressive (or travelling) wave is one in which a disturbance created at one place travels to distant points and keeps travelling unless it is stopped by some external agency. Energy and momentum are transferred from one point of the medium to another, while the particles of the medium themselves merely oscillate about their fixed equilibrium positions and do not move bodily along with the wave.

**Properties** (any four):

1. All the vibrating particles of the medium have the **same amplitude, the same period and the same frequency**.
2. The **state of oscillation, i.e. the phase, changes from particle to particle** along the direction of propagation; a particle further along starts its oscillation later.
3. The wave **transfers energy and momentum** from one point of the medium to another, without any bulk flow of the material of the medium itself.
4. The wave is **doubly periodic** — periodic in time (with period \(T\)) at any one place, and periodic in space (with period \(\lambda\)) at any one instant.
5. Its speed is constant in a given medium and is related to frequency and wavelength by \(\mathrm{v} = n\lambda\).
6. For a mechanical progressive wave the medium must be continuous and elastic, must possess inertia, and must have negligible frictional resistance so that the oscillations are not damped.

| Transverse waves | Longitudinal waves |
|---|---|
| The particles of the medium vibrate in a direction **perpendicular** to the direction of propagation of the wave. | The particles of the medium vibrate in a direction **parallel** to the direction of propagation of the wave. |
| The medium is divided into alternate **crests** (positive displacement) and **troughs** (negative displacement). | The medium is divided into alternate **compressions** (crowded, high pressure) and **rarefactions** (widely separated, low pressure). |
| One cycle is a crest together with the adjacent trough. | One cycle is a compression together with the adjacent rarefaction. |
| The medium must possess **elasticity of shape**, so these waves travel through solids and on the surfaces of liquids only — not through the body of liquids or through gases. | The medium need possess only **elasticity of volume**, so these waves travel through solids, liquids and gases alike (but not through vacuum). |
| There is **no change of pressure or density** at any point; only the shape of the medium changes periodically. | There are **periodic variations of pressure and density** along the path of the wave and with time. |
| They **can be polarised**, because the vibrations can be confined to a single plane. | They **cannot be polarised**, since the direction of vibration is the same as the direction of propagation. |
| Examples: water waves, waves on a stretched string; electromagnetic waves are transverse but need no material medium. | Example: sound waves in air. |

**Newton's formula.** Sound travels through a medium as a succession of compressions and rarefactions, the density of the medium being greater at a compression and smaller at a rarefaction. The velocity of sound must therefore depend on the elasticity and the density of the medium, and Newton wrote the relation as

\[\mathrm{v} = \sqrt{\dfrac{E}{\rho}}\]

where \(E\) is the proper modulus of elasticity of the medium and \(\rho\) its density.

Newton assumed that during the propagation of sound there is **no change in the average temperature** of the medium, i.e. that the process is **isothermal**. The volume elasticity of air determined under an isothermal change is the isothermal bulk modulus, and for a gas this is equal to the pressure \(P\). Hence for air

\[\mathrm{v} = \sqrt{\dfrac{P}{\rho}}\]

Substituting NTP values, with \(P = hdg = 0.76 \times 13600 \times 9.8\) N/m\(^2\) and \(\rho = 1.293\) kg/m\(^3\),

\[\mathrm{v} = \sqrt{\dfrac{0.76 \times 13600 \times 9.8}{1.293}} = 279.9\,\mathrm{m/s}\,\text{at NTP}\]

**Limitation.** The experimentally determined velocity of sound in air at \(0\,^\circ\)C is **332 m/s**, so the measured value is about **16% greater** than the value the formula predicts. A discrepancy of that size is far too large to be attributed to experimental error, and Newton could give no satisfactory explanation of it.

The defect lies in the isothermal assumption. The discrepancy was resolved by Laplace, who pointed out that compressions and rarefactions follow one another far too rapidly for the heat produced to be conducted away, so the process is **adiabatic** rather than isothermal. Replacing the isothermal modulus \(P\) by the adiabatic modulus \(\gamma P\) gives \(\mathrm{v} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma P}{\rho}} = 332.3\) m/s, in close agreement with experiment.

**Given:** speed \(\mathrm{v} = 340\) m/s, wavelength \(\lambda = 1.7\) m.

**a) Frequency.** From the wave relation \(\mathrm{v} = n\lambda\),

\[n = \dfrac{\mathrm{v}}{\lambda} = \dfrac{340}{1.7} = 200\,\mathrm{Hz}\]

**b) Period.** The period is the reciprocal of the frequency,

\[T = \dfrac{1}{n} = \dfrac{1}{200} = 0.005\,\mathrm{s}\]

**Answer:** the frequency is \(200\) Hz and the period is \(0.005\) s (5 ms).

**Given:** frequency \(n = 170\) Hz, wavelength \(\lambda = 2\) m.

The speed, frequency and wavelength of a wave are related by

\[\mathrm{v} = n\lambda\]

\[\therefore \mathrm{v} = 170 \times 2\]

\[\mathrm{v} = 340\,\mathrm{m/s}\]

**Answer:** the speed of sound is \(340\) m/s.

**Given:** time between sending the pulse and receiving the echo \(t = 0.45\) s, speed of sound in water \(\mathrm{v} = 1500\) m/s. Let the depth of the shoal be \(d\).

The sound has to travel **down to the shoal and back again**, so in the time \(t\) it covers a distance \(2d\):

\[2d = \mathrm{v} \times t\]

\[2d = 1500 \times 0.45 = 675\,\mathrm{m}\]

\[\therefore d = \dfrac{675}{2} = 337.5\,\mathrm{m}\]

**Answer:** the shoal is \(337.5\) m below the boat.

(The commonest slip here is to forget the return journey and quote 675 m; the pulse is *received back* at the boat, so the path is a round trip.)

[Textbook answer-key error in part (b), and the book's own part (a) is what convicts it. Part (a) fixes the reading: 60 claps per minute is one clap per second, and the printed \(340\) m/s follows from the sound covering \(2 \times 170\) m in that second. On the same reading 45 claps per minute is an interval of \(\tfrac{4}{3}\) s, so \(2d = 340 \times \tfrac{4}{3}\) and \(d = 226.67\) m. The printed \(255\) m would require an interval of \(1.5\) s, that is 40 claps per minute, not 45 — so the key and the stem cannot both stand. The solution above works from the stem as printed.]

The key idea is that each clap coincides with the echo of the **previous** clap. So the time between two successive claps is exactly the time the sound takes to travel to the wall and back.

**a) Speed of sound.**

Distance to the wall \(d = 170\) m. She makes 60 claps in 1 minute, so the interval between successive claps is

\[t = \dfrac{60\,\mathrm{s}}{60} = 1\,\mathrm{s}\]

In this time the sound covers the round trip \(2d\):

\[\mathrm{v} = \dfrac{2d}{t} = \dfrac{2 \times 170}{1} = 340\,\mathrm{m/s}\]

**b) New distance from the wall.**

The speed of sound is unchanged at \(\mathrm{v} = 340\) m/s. She now makes 45 claps in 1 minute, so the new interval is

\[t' = \dfrac{60}{45} = \dfrac{4}{3}\,\mathrm{s}\]

With \(d'\) the new distance from the wall,

\[2d' = \mathrm{v} \times t' = 340 \times \dfrac{4}{3} = \dfrac{1360}{3} = 453.33\,\mathrm{m}\]

\[\therefore d' = \dfrac{453.33}{2} = 226.67\,\mathrm{m}\]

**Answer:** \(\mathrm{v} = 340\) m/s, and her new distance from the wall is about \(226.67\) m (that is, \(\tfrac{680}{3}\) m).

A useful check: clapping more slowly means the echo takes longer to return, so she must be **further** from the wall than before — and 226.67 m is indeed greater than 170 m, in the ratio \(60:45 = 4:3\).

[Textbook misprint: the second wave's period is printed as \(0.025\) with no unit, where the first wave's carries seconds.]

**Given:** \(T_A = 0.015\) s and \(T_B = 0.025\) s.

Frequency is the reciprocal of the period, \(n = \dfrac{1}{T}\), so

\[n_A = \dfrac{1}{0.015} = 66.67\,\mathrm{Hz}\]

\[n_B = \dfrac{1}{0.025} = 40\,\mathrm{Hz}\]

Since \(66.67 > 40\), **sound wave A has the greater frequency**.

The comparison can in fact be made without any arithmetic: frequency and period are inversely proportional, so the wave with the **shorter** period always has the higher frequency, and \(T_A < T_B\).

[Textbook misprint: this chapter's third exercise block skips item (vi) entirely — its printed list runs i, ii, iii, iv, v, vii, viii, ix, x, xi. The book's own numbering is kept here so the gap stays visible rather than being silently closed up.]

**Given:** \(\mathrm{v} = 1.75\,\mathrm{v}_0\), where \(\mathrm{v}_0\) is the speed of sound at N.T.P., i.e. at \(T_0 = 273\) K.

The speed of sound in a gas is directly proportional to the square root of its absolute temperature:

\[\dfrac{\mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{v}_0} = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{T_0}}\]

Squaring both sides,

\[\dfrac{T}{T_0} = \left(\dfrac{\mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{v}_0}\right)^2 = (1.75)^2 = 3.0625\]

\[\therefore T = 3.0625 \times 273 = 836.06\,\mathrm{K}\]

Converting to the Celsius scale,

\[t = T - 273 = 836.06 - 273 = 563.06\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\]

**Answer:** the temperature must be \(836.06\) K, that is \(563.06\,^\circ\)C.

(Note that the temperature must be taken in **kelvin** throughout — using Celsius in the proportionality would give a quite different and wrong result.)

[Textbook misprint: the stem prints "2 parallel eliffs" for "cliffs" — the same sentence spells the word correctly two lines later — and "He hearns two echos" for "hears two echoes".]

**Given:** the man stands between two parallel cliffs, separated by \(d_1 + d_2 = 1360\) m. He hears the first echo after \(t_1 = 3\) s and the second after \(t_2 = 5\) s.

Let \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) be his distances from the nearer and the farther cliff. Each echo is a round trip to its own cliff and back, so

\[2d_1 = \mathrm{v}\,t_1 \qquad \text{and} \qquad 2d_2 = \mathrm{v}\,t_2\]

Adding the two equations,

\[2(d_1 + d_2) = \mathrm{v}\,(t_1 + t_2)\]

\[2 \times 1360 = \mathrm{v} \times (3 + 5)\]

\[2720 = 8\,\mathrm{v}\]

\[\therefore \mathrm{v} = \dfrac{2720}{8} = 340\,\mathrm{m/s}\]

**Answer:** the speed of sound is \(340\) m/s.

Neither individual distance is needed — adding the two round trips replaces \(d_1 + d_2\) by the given separation. (As a check, the distances themselves come out as \(d_1 = \tfrac{340 \times 3}{2} = 510\) m and \(d_2 = \tfrac{340 \times 5}{2} = 850\) m, and \(510 + 850 = 1360\) m as stated.)

[Textbook misprint: the printed answer reads \(\rho_{dry} = 1.1^{2}\rho_{dry} = 1.21\rho_{moist}\) — the MIDDLE term carries the wrong subscript, so as printed it asserts \(\rho_{dry} = 1.21\rho_{dry}\). The relation intended, and the final one printed, are correct.]

**Given:** the speeds of sound on the two days are in the ratio \(\mathrm{v}_1 : \mathrm{v}_2 = 1 : 1.1\), the temperature being the same on both days.

Since the temperature is unchanged, the difference cannot come from temperature; and at a given place the pressure is essentially the same, so by Laplace's formula \(\mathrm{v} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\gamma P}{\rho}}\) the speed can differ only through the **density** of the air:

\[\mathrm{v} \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\rho}} \qquad \therefore \dfrac{\mathrm{v}_2}{\mathrm{v}_1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\rho_1}{\rho_2}}\]

\[\therefore \dfrac{\rho_1}{\rho_2} = \left(\dfrac{\mathrm{v}_2}{\mathrm{v}_1}\right)^2 = (1.1)^2 = 1.21\]

So the air on the first day (the slower one) is **1.21 times as dense** as the air on the second day.

**Conclusion.** Moist air is always less dense than dry air, because the water vapour in it is lighter than the air it displaces. The day on which sound travelled faster is therefore the day on which the air was **moist**, and the other day the air was comparatively **dry**, with

\[\rho_{dry} = 1.21\,\rho_{moist}\]

Quantitatively, the air on the slower day was 21% denser than on the faster day.

**Given:** emitted frequency \(n_0 = 250\) Hz, speed of the source (the police car) \(\mathrm{v}_s = 15\) m/s, speed of sound \(\mathrm{v} = 340\) m/s, listener stationary so \(\mathrm{v}_L = 0\).

The source is **approaching** the stationary listener, so the denominator takes the minus sign:

\[n = n_0\left[\dfrac{\mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{v} - \mathrm{v}_s}\right]\]

\[n = 250\left[\dfrac{340}{340 - 15}\right]\]

\[n = 250 \times \dfrac{340}{325}\]

\[n = 261.54\,\mathrm{Hz}\]

**Answer:** the recorded frequency is about \(261.54\) Hz.

As expected for relative approach, the recorded frequency is **higher** than the 250 Hz actually emitted.

**Given:** emitted frequency \(n_0 = 1500\) Hz, speed of sound \(\mathrm{v} = 340\) m/s, speed of the ambulance \(\mathrm{v}_s = 30\) m/s, observer stationary so \(\mathrm{v}_L = 0\).

**While the ambulance approaches** (denominator takes the minus sign):

\[n_1 = n_0\left[\dfrac{\mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{v} - \mathrm{v}_s}\right] = 1500\left[\dfrac{340}{340 - 30}\right] = 1500 \times \dfrac{340}{310} = 1645.16\,\mathrm{Hz}\]

**While it recedes** (denominator takes the plus sign):

\[n_2 = n_0\left[\dfrac{\mathrm{v}}{\mathrm{v} + \mathrm{v}_s}\right] = 1500\left[\dfrac{340}{340 + 30}\right] = 1500 \times \dfrac{340}{370} = 1378.38\,\mathrm{Hz}\]

**Difference in the frequencies heard:**

\[\Delta n = n_1 - n_2 = 1645.16 - 1378.38 = 266.78\,\mathrm{Hz}\]

**Answer:** the observer hears a change of about \(266.78\) Hz as the ambulance passes.

Notice that the rise on approach (\(1645.16 - 1500 = 145.16\) Hz) is **not** equal to the fall on recede (\(1500 - 1378.38 = 121.62\) Hz): the Doppler shift is not symmetric about the emitted frequency, because \(\mathrm{v}_s\) enters the denominator.
